DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Noxon (US10767365) in view of Bilton (US8607929) and Goektepe (US20210198817).
With respect to claim 1 Noxon discloses a sound absorbing device (tube trap 100) comprising:
An acoustic resonator( see column 18 , Example 40 described as a Helmholtz resonator) with an opening (inherent in a Helmholtz resonator) and at least one fabric layer (column 3 description of conventional acoustic absorber taught to be present for aesthetic purposes) extending across the opening, the at least one fabric layer comprising fibers with an average pore size.
Bilton discloses the use of a fabric as a part of an acoustical component such that average pore size is known to a results effective variable thereof (abstract).
Goektepe discloses a smart fabric wherein the average pore size is a controllable parameter of an LCE fiber (abstract).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill ion the art before the time of the effective filing to combine the teachings of Bilton that average pore size is a result effective parameter with the fabric of Goektepe so as to control for such a parameter in an acoustic system which is then applied to be a component of the fabric of the fabric cover of Noxon. The motivation for doing so would be to gain the control over the acoustic response in order to enhance the sound reduction.
With respect to claim 2 as it regards the opening being a slit, such openings are known in the art of Helmholtz resonators. Slits, rounded openings, and other shapes are known. The selection of a known type of Helmholtz resonator would have been an obvious matter to one of ordinary skill, and by extension so would the selection of he opening shape.
With respect to claim 3 As it regards the plurality of resonators, this would have constituted only a duplication of the parts of the device. It has been held that mere duplication of the essential working parts of a device involves only routine skill in the art.  St. Regis Paper Co. v. Bemis Co., 193 USPQ 8.
Regarding the fabric layer extending across the openings comprising at least one fabric layer extending across the plurality of openings, this would have been an obvious manner in which to ensure there was a continuity of an element known from Noxon to be an aesthetic consideration in addition to the function requirements of Bilton.
With respect to claims 4  Noxon as modified further discloses ( Goektepe para 0004) the use of reversible actuatable LCE fibers.
With respect to claims 5 and 6 Noxon as modified discloses the invention as claimed except expressly wherein the fibers are electrospun LCE fibers or direct ink wirte LCE fibers. As it regards the selection of these types of LCE fibers, it would have been an obvious matter to select any type of LCE fiber to provide the desired properties of the system. As LCE  fibers are known to be manufactured by different means, the selection of any known means would have been an obvious matter of routine testing.
With respect to claim 7  as it regards the decrease of pore size with increasing temperature, Goektepe (para 16-20) discloses the use of porosity change and that this can be achieved in either direction in response to temperature change. It would have been obvious to select a decrease in porosity with an increase of temperature to absorb greater amount of higher frequency sound at such temperatures.
With respect to claims 8-10 as it regards the selection of the pore size this would have been only a matter of optimization of the device as porose size is known to affect the frequency response of the acoustic system. It has been held that where the general conditions of a claim are disclosed in the prior art, discovering the optimum or working ranges involves only routine skill in the art. In re Aller, 105 USPQ 233.
With respect to claim 11 Noxon as modified (see Goektepe para 16) discloses the provision of a heater configured to heat the fabric. This would have been then obvious to use to decrease the pore size in such a case that it would provide improved acoustic response.
With respect to claim 12 as a heater is disclosed to provide heat in one direction, a cooler would have been an obvious reversal; of this process.
With respect to claim 13 As it regards the provision for a controller to heat and or cool the structure, this would constitute only an automation of the process, as would have been an obvious matter to one of ordinary skill in the art familiar with the taught process of thermo-electric heating.
With respect to claim 14 As Goektepe (para16) discloses thermoelectric heating this implies the presence of at least one electricals wire configured to increase in temperature as claimed. Such a wire is a conventional means of thermo-electric heating.
With respect to claim 15 as it regards the inclusion of a power source, this is further implicit in a thermoelectrical heating system, as would be the case of the controller to automate the system this would have been well understood by one of ordinary skill in the art before the time of the effective filing. This additional limitation would only be the known use of a known structure to provide the thermo-electric heating as taught by Goektepe.
With respect to claim 16 Noxon as modified discloses a sound absorbing device comprising:
An acoustic resonator (Noxon) with an opening and
At least one fabric layer extending across the opening, the at least one fabric layer comprising reversible actuatable LCE fibers (Goektepe) such that an average pore size of the at least one fabric layer increases with decreasing temperature and decreases with increasing temperature (Goektepe discloses the use of temperature to control the porosity in the abstract the application of the teaching to arrive in the desired directions as claimed would have been obvious).
With respect to claim 17 Noxon as modified further discloses a heater (see Goektepe para 16-20) configured to heat the at least one fabric layer, a cooler (obvious reversal of the taught heating) configured to cool the at least one fabric and a controller configured to command the heater and cooler (obvious means of automation).
With respect top claim 18 as it regards the selection fo the pore sizer this would have been an obvious matter based upon the desired results. It has been held that where the general conditions of a claim are disclosed in the prior art, discovering the optimum or working ranges involves only routine skill in the art. In re Aller, 105 USPQ 233.
With respect to claims 19 and 20 Noxon as modified discloses the claimed elements of the sound absorbing device. As to the controller for the heater and cooler, as is discussed above this is only an obvious means of automation. The respective claimed directions for the pore sizer would have been obvious to select as would the pore sizes themselves.
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure. Lee (US20210358468) discloses an acoustic resonating structure with slit opening; Schaake (US20170030610) discloses a flow channel resonator; Fujimori (US8157052) discloses an acoustic resonant structure; Perdue (US7178630) discloses an acoustic device including fabric cover; Gallas (US5444198) discloses a sound trap; and Noxon (US4548292) discloses an acoustical damping structure with fabric cover.
